q: Baking soda and vinegar fizz because their reaction releases which gas?
note: It is the same gas that puts the fizz in soft drinks.

q: Health agencies warn against mixing bleach with ammonia-based cleaners because it releases which toxic gases?
Bleach must never be mixed with acidic toilet cleaners because it can release which toxic gas?
note: Even small amounts can irritate eyes, nose and lungs.

q: In a soap molecule, how is the end attracted to water described?
note: The other end clings to grease, so rinsing water carries the dirt away.

q: Soap molecules trap grease inside tiny spherical clusters. What are these clusters called?
Hard water gets its hardness mainly from dissolved calcium and which other metal?
note: Hard water is what leaves chalky limescale in kettles and on taps.

q: Soap reacts with hard-water minerals to form an insoluble grey deposit. What is it commonly called?
note: Synthetic detergents lather better in hard water because they avoid this reaction.

q: Which type of water hardness can be removed simply by boiling?
note: It comes from dissolved bicarbonates; permanent hardness needs chemical treatment.

q: The black tarnish that forms on silverware is mainly which compound?
note: Eggs, onions and rubber bands can all speed up tarnishing.

q: Besides oxygen, what else does iron need in order to rust?
note: Keeping tools dry and lightly oiled is the simplest way to prevent rust.

q: Why shouldn't vinegar be used to clean marble countertops?
note: Lemon juice damages marble for the same reason.

q: Washing soda, a traditional laundry and cleaning aid, is which chemical compound?
note: It is strongly alkaline, so wearing gloves while using it is a good idea.

q: The reaction of fats or oils with a strong alkali to make soap is called what?
note: Glycerine is produced alongside the soap in this reaction.

q: Mothballs slowly vanish without ever melting. What is this direct solid-to-gas change called?
note: Camphor tablets disappear the same way.

q: Small silica gel packets in new shoes and bags are there to absorb what?
LPG is naturally odourless. Which strong-smelling compound is added so leaks can be noticed?
note: Its smell is often compared to rotten cabbage.

q: If LPG leaks in a kitchen, where does the gas tend to collect?
note: LPG is heavier than air, so low-level ventilation helps clear it.

q: Piped natural gas (PNG) supplied to kitchens is mostly which gas?
Flipping a light switch during a gas leak is risky because it can create what?
note: Safety advice: turn off the regulator and open doors and windows.

q: Hydrogen peroxide is sold in dark bottles because what breaks it down?
note: Heat also speeds up its breakdown, so it is best stored somewhere cool.

q: Household bleach removes colour from stains mainly through which kind of chemical reaction?
note: Many 'colour-safe' bleaches use gentler oxygen-based chemistry instead.

q: A yellow curry stain on a white shirt turns what colour when scrubbed with soap?
note: Soap is alkaline, and the yellow spice pigment acts as a natural indicator.

q: Adding phitkari (alum) to muddy water makes tiny dirt particles clump together. What is this process called?
note: Water treatment plants use the same trick on a much larger scale.

q: On home water purifiers, what does RO stand for?
note: The membrane also strips useful minerals, so some purifiers add them back.

q: On water purifier ads, what does TDS stand for?
note: It is usually measured in milligrams per litre, or ppm.

q: Ordinary kitchen foil is shiny on one side and dull on the other because of what?
a: How it is rolled at the factory
options: How it is rolled at the factory
A wax coating on one side
note: Either side works the same for cooking.

q: When a candle burns, the wax actually burns in which physical state?
note: Molten wax climbs the wick and is vaporised by the flame's heat.

q: Safety matches light only on the box because its striking strip contains which substance?
note: Early matches used toxic white phosphorus and could strike almost anywhere.

q: Ionisation-type smoke alarms contain a tiny amount of which radioactive element?
note: The source is tiny and sealed inside, posing no risk in normal use.

q: Inside a cooking gas cylinder, is LPG stored mostly as a liquid or a gas?
note: It turns back into gas as it leaves the cylinder through the regulator.

q: Rust-resistant 'SS' kitchen utensils contain at least 10.5% of which metal?
note: It forms an invisible oxide film that repairs itself when scratched.

q: Blood stains should be rinsed in cold water because hot water 'cooks' which substance in them?
note: Egg and milk stains respond to cold water for the same reason.

q: Which enzyme in biological detergents breaks down blood and egg stains?
note: Amylase tackles starchy stains, and lipase breaks down greasy ones.

q: The matting and shrinking of wool from heat, soap and rubbing is called what?
note: Wool fibres carry tiny scales that lock together when agitated in warm water.

q: Why do new coloured clothes often bleed dye in their first few washes?
note: Washing new dark clothes separately in cool water reduces bleeding.

q: On a clothing care label, what does a hand in a washtub mean?
On a clothing care label, what does a triangle symbol refer to?
note: A crossed-out triangle means the garment should not be bleached.

q: On a care label, what does a plain circle symbol indicate?
note: A letter inside the circle tells the cleaner which method to use.

q: On a care label, what does a square with a circle inside mean?
note: A square on its own stands for drying in general.

q: On a care label, what do more dots inside the iron symbol mean?
Which of these fabrics can usually take the hottest iron setting?
note: Acrylic and many other synthetics can be ruined by a hot iron.

q: Under ISO care symbols, one dot inside the washtub means a maximum wash temperature of what?
note: Each additional dot allows a hotter wash.

q: A single bar under the washtub symbol on a care label means what?
note: Two bars call for an even gentler cycle, as used for wool.

q: Most of a washing machine's energy use typically goes into doing what?
note: So washing at lower temperatures saves a lot of electricity.

q: Why can frequent fabric softener use make towels less absorbent?
note: Many towel makers suggest using softener sparingly, if at all.

q: Why does a dash of blue (neel) make white clothes look whiter?
note: It is colour correction, not cleaning: blue cancels out a yellowish tinge.

q: Detergent brighteners absorb UV light and give off visible blue light. What is this effect called?
note: It is why white shirts glow under blacklights at parties.

q: Most plastic soft-drink bottles are made from the same polymer family as which clothing fabric?
note: Recycled bottles are often spun into fleece jackets and sportswear.

q: Which number inside the recycling triangle identifies PET plastic?
note: Code 7 is a catch-all for other or mixed plastics.

q: Traditional dry cleaning has most commonly used which solvent?
note: Dry cleaning isn't really dry: clothes are washed in a liquid solvent.

q: Why do dark clothes fade faster when line-dried in the hot sun?
note: Drying dark clothes inside out or in the shade slows fading.

q: Food safety agencies advise keeping a fridge at or below about what temperature?
note: The FDA's equivalent figure is 40°F.

q: What is the standard recommended temperature for a home freezer?
note: That works out to roughly 0°F.

q: Food safety's 'danger zone', where bacteria multiply fastest, runs from about 5°C up to what?
note: Hot food should be kept above this range until it is served.

q: Does freezing food kill most of the bacteria in it?
a: No, it only stops them growing
options: No, it only stops them growing
Yes, it kills all of them
note: Bacteria can become active again once the food thaws.

q: Per USDA advice, raw meat thawed in which way can be safely refrozen without cooking?
options: In a bowl of cold water
note: Refreezing may cost some texture, but it stays safe if kept cold.

q: Cooked leftovers should be refrigerated within how many hours, according to the USDA?
note: In weather above 32°C, the USDA shortens this to one hour.

q: At full pressure, water inside a pressure cooker can reach about what temperature?
note: In an open pan at sea level, water can't get much hotter than 100°C.

q: Why does food cook faster in a pressure cooker?
a: Higher pressure raises the boiling point
options: Higher pressure raises the boiling point

q: In a high-altitude town like Leh, water boils at what temperature compared with sea level?
note: So cooking takes longer in the mountains.

q: Microwave ovens heat food mainly by making molecules of which substance vibrate?
note: Very dry foods heat up much more slowly in a microwave.

q: Crumpled aluminium foil should never go in a running microwave oven because it can cause what?
Why can't the cooking waves escape through the small holes in a microwave oven's door mesh?
a: The holes are smaller than the wavelength
options: The glass absorbs all of them
The holes are smaller than the wavelength
note: The waves are about 12 cm long; the holes are only millimetres wide.

q: For a pan to work on an induction cooktop, what should cling firmly to its base?
note: Cast iron works well; plain aluminium or copper pans won't heat.

q: An induction cooktop heats a pan by inducing what kind of electric currents in its base?
Non-stick pans are often coated with PTFE, best known by which brand name?
note: PTFE was discovered by accident at DuPont in 1938.

q: Why does a steel spoon feel colder than a wooden one at the same room temperature?
options: Steel absorbs cold from the air
note: Both spoons really are at the same temperature.

q: A vacuum flask's vacuum gap mainly blocks heat transfer by which two processes?
note: Its silvered inner walls cut down heat transfer by radiation.

q: Which scientist invented the vacuum flask in 1892?
note: He never patented it, and others later made money selling it.

q: Which button on a kitchen scale resets it to ignore the bowl's weight?
note: Tare is an old trade term for the weight of a container.

q: In standard cooking measures, a teaspoon holds about how many millilitres?
note: In most countries a tablespoon holds 15 ml.

q: Bacteria spreading from raw meat to ready-to-eat food via knives or boards is called what?
note: Separate chopping boards for raw meat help prevent it.

q: Why do food safety agencies advise against washing raw chicken?
note: Thorough cooking, not rinsing, is what kills the bacteria.

q: The CDC advises scrubbing hands with soap for at least how many seconds?
note: Humming 'Happy Birthday' twice is the classic timer.

q: The CDC says alcohol hand sanitiser should contain at least what percentage of alcohol?
note: Soap and water work better when hands are visibly dirty or greasy.

q: What does a 'best before' date on packaged food mainly indicate?
note: 'Use by' dates are about safety and should be followed strictly.

q: Which type of refrigerator needs occasional manual defrosting?
note: Frost-free models use a fan and timed heater to stop ice building up.

q: What are the warm coils on the back of a fridge doing?
note: So fridges need a gap from the wall to run efficiently.

q: In older fridges, why is the freezer compartment usually placed at the top?
options: Warm air collects at the bottom

q: In many pressure cookers, what does the safety valve's metal plug do if pressure builds dangerously?
note: It is a backup in case the main vent or whistle gets blocked.

q: Which type of glass, used in lab beakers and ovenware, resists cracking from sudden temperature changes?
note: The Indian brand Borosil takes its name from it.

q: Hot water helps loosen a stuck metal jar lid because the metal does what?
note: Metal grows more than glass when heated, so the lid loosens.

q: Ice floats on water because it has a lower what?
note: Most substances are denser as solids; water is a rare exception.

q: At about what temperature is liquid water at its densest?
note: So deep lake water tends to stay near this temperature in winter.

q: By roughly how much does water's volume increase when it freezes?
note: This expansion is why water pipes can burst in freezing weather.

q: A clay matka keeps drinking water cool mainly through which process?
note: Water seeps through tiny pores and takes heat with it as it dries off.

q: Does a ceiling fan lower the air temperature of a room?
a: No, it only cools your skin
options: No, it only cools your skin
Yes, by pulling in cold air
note: Moving air carries heat away from your body faster.

q: Water droplets forming on the outside of a glass of cold water come from which process?
note: The droplets come from the surrounding air, not through the glass.

q: Moving water out of a tank using a tube that runs up over the rim and down is called what?
note: The tube's outlet must sit lower than the water surface for it to work.

q: Door handles sit far from the hinges to get the most of which turning effect?
note: The same push turns the door more easily the farther it is from the pivot.

q: A sharp knife cuts better because its force acts on a tiny area, creating more what?
note: Pressure equals force divided by area.

q: Why do static shocks from door handles happen more often in dry weather?
a: Dry air lets charge build up
options: Metal gets colder in dry weather
Dry air lets charge build up
note: Humid air helps charge leak away gradually.

q: Woollen sweaters keep you warm mainly by trapping what?
note: Trapped air is a poor conductor, so body heat escapes slowly.

q: Why do black clothes feel hotter in sunshine than white ones?
note: White reflects most visible light back.

q: Steam at 100°C scalds worse than boiling water mainly because of what extra hidden energy?
note: Steam gives up this extra energy as it turns back into water on skin.

q: Soap bubbles show swirling rainbow colours because of which light effect?
note: The colours shift as the bubble wall thins just before it pops.

q: Many electric kettles switch off using a part made of two bonded metals that bends when hot. What is it?
note: The same trick was used in old electric irons and room thermostats.

q: Why don't birds sitting on a single live power line get a shock?
a: No voltage difference across their body
options: No voltage difference across their body
note: Touching a second wire or a pole at the same time would let current flow through them.

q: Which of these metals is most widely used for household electrical wiring?
Shaving and makeup mirrors that show a magnified face are which type of mirror?
note: Car side mirrors do the opposite, bulging outward to show a wider view.

q: Which instrument measures the humidity of the air in a room?
Desert coolers cool a room best in which kind of weather?
note: In muggy, humid weather their cooling effect drops sharply.

q: Why do aerosol cans warn against heating or burning them?
a: Pressure inside can make them burst
options: Pressure inside can make them burst

q: What does MCB stand for in a home's electrical panel?
note: It has largely replaced rewirable fuses in newer homes.

q: Besides overloads, what electrical fault does an MCB protect against?
note: Once the fault is fixed, it can simply be switched back on.

q: What does an RCCB detect before it trips?
note: It compares current in the live and neutral wires and trips on any mismatch.

q: RCCBs meant to protect people from shocks typically trip at what leakage current?
note: They usually cut the power within a fraction of a second.

q: In a traditional fuse, what happens to the thin wire when too much current flows?
note: Many older Indian homes had porcelain 'kit-kat' fuses with replaceable wire.

q: What is the main safety job of the earth wire in home wiring?
a: Carrying fault current safely to ground
options: Carrying fault current safely to ground

q: Under the international IEC colour code, the earth wire is green striped with which colour?
note: In the same code, live is brown and neutral is blue.

q: On an Indian 3-pin plug, which pin is the thickest and longest?
note: Being longest, it connects first and disconnects last.

q: What is the standard nominal mains voltage for homes in India?
At what frequency does India's mains electricity supply alternate?
note: That means the current changes direction 100 times every second.

q: India's large 15 A round 3-pin plug, used for geysers and ACs, is which IEC plug type?
note: The smaller 5 A 3-pin plug common in Indian homes is Type D.

q: On an Indian electricity bill, one 'unit' of consumption equals what?
How many hours can a 100-watt bulb run on one kilowatt-hour?
note: A 10-watt LED could run for 100 hours on the same kilowatt-hour.

q: Is a kilowatt-hour a unit of power or of energy?
note: The watt measures power, the rate at which energy is used.

q: Why do LED bulbs use less electricity than filament bulbs for the same light?
a: They waste less energy as heat
options: They waste less energy as heat
They glow only part of the time
They store light during the day
note: Old filament bulbs turned roughly 90% of their energy into heat.

q: What does LED stand for?
Compact fluorescent lamps (CFLs) contain a small amount of which toxic metal?
note: So broken CFLs need careful clean-up and proper disposal.

q: Old incandescent bulbs glow thanks to a thin filament of which metal?
note: It has the highest melting point of any metal.

q: A home inverter converts a battery's stored energy into which type of current for appliances?
note: Batteries supply direct current, while home sockets deliver alternating current.

q: On a power backup unit for PCs, what does UPS stand for?
What is the power drawn by devices that are switched off but still plugged in commonly called?
note: Switching off at the socket avoids it.

q: A voltage stabiliser for a fridge or AC mainly protects it against what?
In an inverter AC, which main component varies its speed instead of switching fully on and off?
note: Working steadily at lower speed uses less electricity than frequent stop-starts.

q: Why is it risky to touch electrical switches with wet hands?
If someone is stuck to a live appliance, what should you do first?
note: Touching them directly could pass the current into you too.

q: Electrical wires are coated in plastic because plastic is a good what?
What does BEE stand for on Indian appliance star labels?
note: It was set up in 2002 under the Energy Conservation Act, 2001.

q: BEE star labels rate appliances from 1 star up to how many stars?
note: More stars means lower energy use for a similar appliance.

q: A BEE star label on a fridge shows its estimated electricity use per what time period?
BEE star ratings for room air conditioners are based on which efficiency measure?
note: It stands for Indian Seasonal Energy Efficiency Ratio.

q: A '1-ton' air conditioner removes heat at about how many BTU per hour?
note: The 'ton' comes from the cooling effect of a ton of ice thawing over a day.

q: Under a BEE rule effective January 2020, what default temperature must new room ACs in India be set to?
note: Users can still change it; only the factory default is fixed.

q: On BIS-hallmarked gold jewellery, which number indicates 22-carat purity?
note: It means the gold is 91.6% pure.

q: Roughly what percentage of 18-carat gold is pure gold?
What does HUID stand for on hallmarked gold jewellery in India?
note: Each piece gets its own six-character alphanumeric code.

q: As a gemstone weight, one carat equals how many milligrams?
note: The gold 'karat' measures purity, not weight.

q: What is the recommended first aid for a minor burn?
a: Hold it under cool tap water
options: Hold it under cool tap water
note: Butter, ice and toothpaste can all make a burn worse.

q: The recovery position is for someone who is unconscious but still doing what?
note: It keeps the airway open and lets fluids drain from the mouth.

q: Adult CPR chest compressions should be given at about what rate per minute?
note: Each compression should press the chest down at least 5 cm.

q: For a nosebleed, first-aid guidance says to sit and lean in which direction?
note: Tilting back can send blood down the throat.

q: Abdominal thrusts for a choking person are popularly named after which American surgeon?
What does AED stand for, the portable device used on someone in cardiac arrest?
note: It gives spoken instructions, so untrained bystanders can use it.

q: If a household chemical splashes into someone's eye, what should you do first?
note: Keep flushing for a good while, then get medical help.

q: Should you make someone vomit after they swallow a household cleaner?
note: Corrosive liquids can cause more damage coming back up.

q: Burning coal in a closed room is dangerous mainly because it gives off which odourless gas?
note: Keep rooms ventilated when using angithis or heaters.
